newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenyan reform groups press on with Mombasa rally.
newsitem.headline: Kenyan reform groups press on with Mombasa rally.

text.p: A crisis over constitutional reforms in Kenya deepened on Thursday, with reform groups planning more demonstrations and a skirmish outside parliament between youths.

Some 50 stone-throwing youths shouting slogans in support of the ruling Kenya African National Union (KANU) party clashed with 50 youths allied to opposition parties outside parliament in the capital.

Three people including a policeman were injured by stones and witnesses said police inside the parliament compound fired five times in the air to disperse the opposition supporters. It was unclear if the firing was blanks or live ammunition.
Riot police later chased the youths away from parliament.

The National Convention Executive Council (NCEC), an alliance of opposition parties, civic groups and other bodies demanding constitutional reforms, earlier said it would go ahead with a rally in the Indian Ocean city of Mombasa on Saturday.

But after days of wrangling with authorities over who would be involved in any dialogue on reforms, some NCEC members said the only way ahead was to resume pressure on the government through more conflict between riot police and demonstrators.
The reforms demanded by the NCEC would reduce the power of President Daniel arap Moi, 73 and in power for 13 years. No date is set for presidential and parliamentary polls this year.
"The only way out of this is more violence," said Otieno K'Opiyo, an opposition FORD-Kenya parliamentarian. "Our capacity to do damage is still there. It is the only course we have."
The Indian Ocean city of Mombasa is at the heart of Kenya's tourism industry, its main source of foreign revenue and its leading employer. It is also Kenya's main port and second city.
The NCEC said KANU, headed by Moi, appeared to be inviting confrontation by refusing to open dialogue with it on reforms.

But it was unclear if police would again ruthlessly suppress the rally and thus damage tourism and scare off foreign investors or whether popular support for the campaign had been dented by Moi agreeing on July 17 to make some reforms.

In a move to calm nervous markets, Moi reappointed Central Bank Governor Micah Cheserem on Thursday for four more years. On Wednesday, Cheserem said he believed trouble would be avoided if police did not intervene forcibly to break up rallies in Kenya.
"The consequences of such confrontation for the economy and political stability are too ghastly for a ruling party to promote," the NCEC said in a statement at a news conference.
"The National Executive Council will continue with its mass action programmes until the government takes measures which show that it is interested in a genuine dialogue," it warned.

A senior government official said on Thursday private Kenyan constitutional experts had been brought in to draft legislation to set up a constitutional review commission and to repeal or amend 11 laws the opposition demands scrapped before polls.
The concession by Moi on some reforms aimed at pulling the reform rug out from under the opposition-backed alliance, which has forged rare unity among all his usually divided opponents.

KANU Secretary-General Joseph Kamotho, who is also education minister, said on Wednesday KANU would not discuss reforms with the NCEC because it was an un-elected body. The NCEC said it had a popular mandate and still believed Moi wanted talks with it.
At least nine people were killed in Kenya on July 7 during conflict in Nairobi and other cities and towns when riot police violently broke up several demonstrations called by the NCEC.
